How can we answer this question?

# US Social Security Data

Public dataset containing baby names and registered **biological sex**.

## Understanding the Context

In this course, you will search for interesting datasets to work with and learn about different data sources on your own. **It is super important to read data documentation!**

Reading from the [Social Security Administration (SSA) Background Description](https://www.ssa.gov/oact/babynames/background.html):

> *"All names are from Social Security card applications for births that occurred in the United States after 1879. Note that many people born before 1937 never applied for a Social Security card, so their names are not included in our data. For others who did apply, our records may not show the place of birth, and again their names are not included in our data."*
>
> *"The data we are using below are from a 100% sample of the records on Social Security card applications as of end of year when the database was last updated."*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Get Data Programmatically

This automated pipeline downloads the zip file directly from `ssa.gov`, unzips it, and consolidates all single-year data files into one master data table (tibble). Because the SSA updates this database annually, running this code will automatically fetch the most recent data each year.

```{r}
#| label: download-data

# Download zip file directly from SSA if it doesn't already exist locally
data_url  <- "https://www.ssa.gov/oact/babynames/names.zip"
local_zip <- "names.zip"

if (!file.exists(local_zip)) {
  download.file(data_url, destfile = local_zip, mode = "wb")
}

# Unzip all contents into a temporary directory
temp_dir <- tempfile()
dir.create(temp_dir)
unzip(local_zip, exdir = temp_dir)

# Identify all single-year .txt files
txt_files <- list.files(temp_dir, pattern = "^yob.*\\.txt$", full.names = TRUE)

# Read each year's file and combine into a single tibble
babynames_list <- lapply(txt_files, function(file_path) {
  # Extract year from filename (e.g., "yob1880.txt" -> 1880)
  year_val <- as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9]", "", basename(file_path)))

  df <- read.csv(
    file_path,
    header = FALSE,
    col.names = c("Name", "Sex", "Count"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  df$Year <- year_val
  return(df)
})

# Bind into a single tibble
babynames <- bind_rows(babynames_list) |>
  as_tibble()

# Display our master dataset
babynames

```

## Data Cleaning & Exploration

This data is already very clean, requiring minimal initial wrangling.

```{r}

babynames
```

```{r}

dim(babynames)
```

```{r}

```

```{r}

# Pick a name and sex (M or F) to plot popularity over time
target_name <- "jenna"
target_sex  <- "F"

babynames |> 
  filter(Name == target_name, Sex == target_sex) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = Count)) +

```

# Summarizing Data

### How many total babies were registered each year?

We use `group_by()` and `summarize()` to aggregate data by group.

```{r}
#| label: count-babies-by-year

# Summarize total counts by Year and Sex
year_sex_counts <- babynames |> 
  group_by(Year, Sex) |> 
  summarize(TotalCount = sum(Count), .groups = "drop")

year_sex_counts
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-babies-by-year

# Plot total baby registrations over time by Sex
year_sex_counts |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = TotalCount, color = Sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Baby Registrations by Year and Sex",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Number of Babies"
  )
```

### How many unique names were used each year?

```{r}
#| label: unique-names-by-year

# Count distinct names per Year and Sex
year_unique_names <- babynames |> 
  group_by(Year, Sex) |> 
  summarize(UniqueNames = n_distinct(Name), .groups = "drop")

year_unique_names
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-unique-names

# Plot count of unique names over time
year_unique_names |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = UniqueNames, color = Sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Unique Baby Names by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Count of Unique Names"
  )
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Compute Proportion of Female Babies for Each Name

```{r}
#| label: proportion-female-per-name

# Summarize total counts across all years for each name by sex
sex_counts <- babynames |> 
  group_by(Name, Sex) |> 
  summarize(TotalCount = sum(Count), .groups = "drop") |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = Sex, values_from = TotalCount, values_fill = 0) |> 
  mutate(
    Total = F + M,
    PropFemale = F / Total
  )

sex_counts
```

# Build a Simple Classifier (Model)

We write a function that takes a first name and returns `"F"`, `"M"`, or `"Unknown"` based on historical data.

```{r}
#| label: classifier-function

sex_from_name <- function(input_name, reference_df = sex_counts) {
  clean_name <- str_to_lower(input_name)
  match <- reference_df |> filter(Name == clean_name)
  
  if (nrow(match) == 0) {
    return("Unknown")
  } else if (match$PropFemale > 0.5) {
    return("F")
  } else {
    return("M")
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: test-classifier

# Test a name using our classifier function
sex_from_name("alex")
```

# Student Roster Analysis

### What fraction of people in this class have names in the SSA Database?

Let's load class roster data from Canvas/Registrar.

```{r}
#| label: load-roster

# Load student roster CSV
names_df <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/suchen1221/UTSDS_data_science_class/refs/heads/main/data/SDS313_names.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> 
  mutate(
    FirstName = str_to_lower(`FirstName`),
  )

cat("Number of people in class:", nrow(names_df), "\n")
head(names_df)
```

```{r}
#| label: compute-roster-overlap

# Calculate the fraction of class first names present in SSA database
in_database <- names_df$FirstName %in% sex_counts$Name
cat("Fraction of names in the baby names data:", round(mean(in_database), 2), "\n")
```

### Which names are missing from the Database?

Why might certain names not appear?

```{r}
#| label: identify-missing-names

missing_names <- names_df |> 
  filter(!FirstName %in% sex_counts$Name) |> 
  pull(FirstName) |> 
  unique()

missing_names
```

# Predict Sex for the Class

- **Input:** First Name
- **Model:** `sex_from_name`
- **Output:** Predicted Sex (`F`, `M`, or `Unknown`)

```{r}
#| label: apply-predictions

names_df <- names_df |> 
  mutate(PredictedSex = map_chr(FirstName, sex_from_name))

names_df
```

### Estimate Proportion of Female Students

```{r}
#| label: estimate-female-proportion

# Estimate fraction of female students (excluding 'Unknown' predictions)
known_predictions <- names_df |> filter(PredictedSex != "Unknown")
pred_prob_female   <- mean(known_predictions$PredictedSex == "F")

pred_prob_female
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Using Simulation to Estimate Uncertainty

Suppose `name1` has a female proportion of $0.50000001$ ($50.000001\%$) and `name2` has a female proportion of $0.49999999$ ($49.999999\%$). A deterministic $0.5$ threshold predicts `name1` as `F` and `name2` as `M`, despite virtually identical historical distributions!

Instead of a hard threshold, we can simulate predictions probabilistically: assign `F` with probability $p$ (where $p = \text{PropFemale}$) and `M` with probability $1 - p$.

```{r}
#| label: extract-class-probabilities

# Filter database to matches from our class roster
class_probabilities <- sex_counts |> 
  filter(Name %in% names_df$FirstName)

class_probabilities
```

### Demonstrating Probabilistic Sampling

```{r}
#| label: single-sample-demo

# Pick a single probability p and sample one result
fp <- 0.5
mp <- 1 - fp

sample(c("F", "M"), size = 10, replace = TRUE, prob = c(fp, mp))
```

### Single Class Simulation

```{r}
#| label: class-simulation-single

# Simulate predicted sex for each student once using a simple loop
predict_sex <- c()

for (i in 1:nrow(class_probabilities)) {
  fp <- class_probabilities$PropFemale[i]
  mp <- 1 - fp
  
  simulated_sex <- sample(c("F", "M"), size = 1, prob = c(fp, mp))
  predict_sex   <- c(predict_sex, simulated_sex)
}

# Calculate predicted female proportion in class for this single simulation
mean(predict_sex == "F")
```

### Running Monte Carlo Simulations ($10,000$ iterations)

```{r}
#| label: simulation-function

# Function that performs one simulation pass over the class
simulate_female_prop <- function(class_df) {
  predict_sex <- c()
  
  for (i in 1:nrow(class_df)) {
    fp <- class_df$PropFemale[i]
    mp <- 1 - fp
    simulated_sex <- sample(c("F", "M"), size = 1, prob = c(fp, mp))
    predict_sex   <- c(predict_sex, simulated_sex)
  }
  
  return(mean(predict_sex == "F"))
}

# Test function once
simulate_female_prop(class_probabilities)
```

```{r}
#| label: run-monte-carlo

# Repeat simulation 10,000 times
n_reps <- 10000
simulations <- numeric(n_reps)

set.seed(313) # For reproducibility

for (n in 1:n_reps) {
  simulations[n] <- simulate_female_prop(class_probabilities)
}

head(simulations)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-simulation-results

# Visualize distribution of simulation results
tibble(FemaleProp = simulations) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = FemaleProp)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", binwidth = 0.02) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimated % of Female Students in SDS 313 (10,000 Simulations)",
    x = "Simulated Proportion Female",
    y = "Number of Simulations"
  )
```
